edges.description: Bright visual stimulation evokes larger visual-cortical responses in photic sneezers.
edges.target: Enhanced Visual and Somatosensory Cortical Responses

edges.description: The optic-trigeminal model proposes that the visual signal cross-activates trigeminal pathways.
The parasympathetic model proposes spread from the pupillary response into nasal autonomic pathways.
Cortical somatosensory activation is associated with the subjective nasal prickle that can accompany PSR.
edges.source: Enhanced Visual and Somatosensory Cortical Responses

edges.description: The cortical model proposes that enhanced sensory processing recruits downstream sneeze-execution circuitry.
edges.source: Enhanced Visual and Somatosensory Cortical Responses

edges.description: The hypothesis predicts that cross-activated trigeminal signaling recruits the sneeze-execution circuit.
The hypothesis predicts that nasal autonomic changes recruit the general sneeze circuit.
Activation of the final sneeze-execution pathway produces the sneeze motor response; photic recruitment is inferred rather than directly tested.

nodes.description: A sudden transition to bright light is the defining external stimulus. The intensity, spectrum, duration, timing, and spatial configuration sufficient to elicit PSR have not been established parametrically.

evidence.reference_title: Stimulus conditions eliciting sneezing in response to bright light.
evidence.snippet: The reviewed studies, including four case reports and three laboratory experiments, consistently support that bright light can induce sneezing in susceptible individuals.

nodes.description: Compared with controls, photic sneezers show enhanced visual-cortical excitability; stronger nose-prickling is associated with insular and secondary somatosensory activation. These are human neural correlates, not a demonstrated complete causal pathway.
nodes.id: Enhanced Visual and Somatosensory Cortical Responses

evidence.reference_title: When the sun prickles your nose: an EEG study identifying neural bases of photic sneezing.
evidence.snippet: we found a generally enhanced excitability of the visual cortex (mainly in the cuneus) to visual stimuli in 'photic sneezers' compared with control subjects

evidence.reference_title: When the sun prickles your nose: an EEG study identifying neural bases of photic sneezing.
evidence.snippet: a stronger prickling sensation in the nose of photic sneezers was found to be associated with activation in the insula and stronger activation in the secondary somatosensory cortex

nodes.description: In experimental studies of the general sneeze reflex, neuromedin B signaling from nasal sensory neurons activates NMB-receptor-expressing neurons in a brainstem sneeze-evoking region, which project to the caudal ventral respiratory group. Recruitment of this circuit by photic stimulation has not been directly tested.

evidence.reference_title: Sneezing reflex is mediated by a peptidergic pathway from nose to brainstem.
evidence.snippet: neuromedin B (NMB) peptide is essential for signaling sneezing. Ablation of NMB-sensitive postsynaptic neurons in the sneeze-evoking region or deficiency in NMB receptor abolished the sneezing reflex.

nodes.description: Involuntary sneezing after sudden exposure to bright light.

evidence.reference_title: A genome-wide association study on photic sneeze reflex in the Chinese population.
evidence.snippet: Photic sneeze reflex (PSR) is an interesting but yet mysterious phenotype featured by individuals' response of sneezing in exposure to bright light.

nodes.description: A subjective nose-prickling sensation can accompany photic stimulation; available studies do not establish a population frequency.

evidence.reference_title: When the sun prickles your nose: an EEG study identifying neural bases of photic sneezing.
evidence.snippet: Exposure to bright light such as sunlight elicits a sneeze or prickling sensation in about one of every four individuals.

nodes.description: A hypothesized central convergence permits activity in optic pathways to cross-activate trigeminal pathways and generate nasal sensation. No solid anatomical or functional evidence currently validates this PSR pathway.

evidence.reference_title: Stimulus conditions eliciting sneezing in response to bright light.
evidence.snippet: there is no solid anatomical or functional evidence base that would arbitrate between these distinct neuroanatomical theories.

nodes.description: A hypothesized spread of strong light-evoked parasympathetic activity into nasal secretomotor pathways produces secretion or tickling that then triggers a sneeze. Direct PSR evidence is lacking.

evidence.reference_title: Stimulus conditions eliciting sneezing in response to bright light.
evidence.snippet: there is no solid anatomical or functional evidence base that would arbitrate between these distinct neuroanatomical theories.
